specStatements.text: matter is composed of tiny particles called atoms and there are about 100 different naturally occurring types of atoms called elements
elements show periodic relationships in their chemical and physical properties
these periodic properties can be explained in terms of the atomic structure of the elements
atoms bond by either transferring electrons from one atom to another or by sharing electrons
the shapes of molecules (groups of atoms bonded together) and the way giant structures are arranged is of great importance in terms of the way they behave
there are barriers to reaction so reactions occur at different rates
chemical reactions take place in only three different ways:
energy is conserved in chemical reactions so can therefore be neither created or destroyed.

scopeNotes.statement: chemical reactions take place in only three different ways:
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Only the three ways the specification then names are taught - proton transfer, electron transfer and electron sharing. No fourth category is invented, and no reaction-mechanism language beyond these three is used. Classification questions use only reactions whose category is unambiguous at GCSE (acid-alkali neutralisation for proton transfer, metal with non-metal or displacement for electron transfer, non-metal with non-metal forming covalent bonds for electron sharing); students are never asked to sort a borderline case.

scopeNotes.statement: matter is composed of tiny particles called atoms and there are about 100 different naturally occurring types of atoms called elements
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The number is kept as the specification gives it - about 100, naturally occurring. No exact count of natural elements is asserted, and the synthetic elements are mentioned only to the extent needed to honour the word 'naturally occurring'. Nothing is taught about how synthetic elements are made or named.

scopeNotes.statement: the shapes of molecules (groups of atoms bonded together) and the way giant structures are arranged is of great importance in terms of the way they behave
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Shape and arrangement are treated at the level the specification uses - simple molecular versus giant ionic, giant covalent and metallic structures, and the consequences for melting point, hardness and conductivity. No bond angles, no VSEPR theory and no formal names for molecular geometry are introduced, because the specification asks about the importance of shape and arrangement to behaviour, not about predicting geometry.

scopeNotes.statement: there are barriers to reaction so reactions occur at different rates
scopeNotes.howHonoured: The barrier is treated qualitatively as activation energy - the minimum energy colliding particles must have - and rate is treated through collision frequency and the proportion of collisions with enough energy. No Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution curves, no rate equations and no orders of reaction are introduced, none of which appear in this specification.

scopeNotes.statement: energy is conserved in chemical reactions so can therefore be neither created or destroyed.
scopeNotes.howHonoured: Conservation is taught qualitatively: energy is transferred between the reacting chemicals and the surroundings, which is why exothermic reactions warm the surroundings and endothermic reactions cool them. Bond energy calculations are not used here, because they are Higher tier content in 4.5.1.3 while every statement in 4.11 is common to both tiers, and marking such material 'both' would misrepresent the tiering.

concepts.definition: The tiny particle from which all matter is composed. An atom is the smallest part of an element that can still exist as that element.
A substance made of only one type of atom. There are about 100 different naturally occurring types of atom, and each type of atom is an element; the elements are set out in the periodic table.

A substance containing the atoms of two or more elements chemically combined in fixed proportions. Because about 100 elements can combine in an enormous number of ratios and arrangements, millions of different compounds exist.

The pattern by which similar chemical and physical properties recur at regular intervals when the elements are arranged in order of atomic number. This repeating pattern is what the word 'periodic' in periodic table refers to.
A vertical column of the periodic table. Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, which is why they have similar chemical properties.
A horizontal row of the periodic table. Elements in the same period have the same number of occupied electron shells, and their properties change steadily across the row rather than staying similar.

The arrangement of the electrons in shells around the nucleus of an atom. It is this arrangement, and above all the number of electrons in the outer shell, that explains the periodic properties of the elements.

Bonding formed when electrons are transferred from a metal atom to a non-metal atom. The oppositely charged ions produced are held together by strong electrostatic forces of attraction acting in all directions.
Bonding formed when two non-metal atoms share a pair of electrons. The shared pair is attracted to both nuclei at once, which is what holds the atoms together, and covalent bonds are strong.
An atom, or a group of atoms, that has lost or gained electrons and so carries an overall electrical charge. Losing electrons gives a positive ion; gaining electrons gives a negative ion.
A group of atoms bonded together by covalent bonds. The size and shape of a molecule, and the strength of the forces between one molecule and the next, affect how the substance behaves.

A structure in which very large numbers of atoms or ions are joined by a regular repeating network of strong bonds. Giant ionic lattices, giant covalent structures such as diamond and graphite, and metals are all giant structures.

The idea that the way the particles of a substance are arranged, and the strength of the forces holding them in place, decide its properties - its melting and boiling points, its hardness, and whether it conducts electricity.
The minimum amount of energy that particles must have in order to react when they collide. It is the barrier to reaction: collisions with less than this energy do not lead to any chemical change.

How quickly reactants are used up or products are formed. Because different reactions have different energy barriers, and because conditions such as temperature, concentration and surface area differ, reactions occur at very different rates.
A substance that increases the rate of a reaction by providing a different reaction pathway with a lower activation energy. A catalyst is not used up during the reaction.

A chemical change in which a hydrogen ion, H+, is passed from one substance to another. A hydrogen ion is a hydrogen atom that has lost its only electron, so it is a single proton; acid reactions with alkalis and bases work this way.
A chemical change in which electrons pass from one substance to another. Loss of electrons is oxidation and gain of electrons is reduction; the reaction of a metal with a non-metal works this way.
A chemical change in which atoms form covalent bonds by sharing pairs of electrons, rather than by giving electrons up or taking them. Reactions between non-metal elements work this way.

The principle that energy can be neither created nor destroyed. In a chemical reaction energy is only transferred, so the total amount of energy before the reaction equals the total amount afterwards.

An exothermic reaction transfers energy to the surroundings, so the temperature of the surroundings rises. An endothermic reaction takes in energy from the surroundings, so their temperature falls. In neither case is energy made or lost.

concepts.term: The three ways reactions take place
concepts.definition: Chemical reactions take place in only three different ways: proton transfer, electron transfer and electron sharing. The many familiar names for reactions describe patterns, but underneath each is one of these three changes.

misconceptions.question: If there are only about 100 elements, how can there be millions of different substances?
misconceptions.correct: About 100 types of atom can be combined in a vast number of ratios and arrangements, and each different combination is a different compound.
misconceptions.misconception: There must only be about 100 different substances in the world, because there are only about 100 different types of atom to make them from.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students meet 'about 100 elements' as a striking fact and read it as a limit on substances rather than a limit on ingredients. The combinatorial step - that a small set of building blocks gives an unlimited set of products - is rarely made explicit.
misconceptions.correction: Think of the elements as an alphabet. Around 26 letters give an unlimited number of words; around 100 types of atom give millions of compounds, because atoms can join in different numbers, different ratios and different arrangements.

misconceptions.question: Do all of the elements shown in the periodic table occur naturally?
misconceptions.correct: There are about 100 naturally occurring types of atom; the remaining elements in the table have been made artificially.
misconceptions.misconception: Every element printed in the periodic table is found somewhere in nature, so the number of naturally occurring elements is the same as the number of boxes in the table.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The periodic table is presented as a single finished object, with no visual distinction between elements dug out of the ground and elements made in a laboratory a few atoms at a time.
misconceptions.correction: The specification says about 100 naturally occurring types of atom. The heaviest elements at the bottom of the table were made artificially and are not found naturally, so the table contains more elements than nature supplies.

misconceptions.question: Oxygen gas exists as O2 molecules. Is oxygen still an element?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. An element is a substance made of only one type of atom, whether those atoms are separate or bonded together in molecules.
misconceptions.misconception: If the particles are molecules rather than single atoms, the substance cannot be an element - it must be a compound because the atoms are joined together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn 'element = one type of atom' and 'compound = atoms joined together', then treat any joining as evidence of a compound. Diagrams that draw elements as lone circles reinforce this.
misconceptions.correction: Test the atoms, not the joins. O2 contains only oxygen atoms, so it is an element. CO2 contains carbon and oxygen atoms chemically combined, so it is a compound.

misconceptions.question: Sodium, magnesium and aluminium are next to each other in the table. Should they react in similar ways?
misconceptions.correct: No. They are in the same period but different groups, and it is the group, not the period, that gives similar chemical properties.
misconceptions.misconception: Elements close together in the periodic table have similar properties, so neighbours in a row behave like each other in reactions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Similar properties' is remembered as 'near each other', without the direction being pinned down, and rows are read first because English text is read left to right.
misconceptions.correction: Read the table in columns for chemistry. Elements in a group share the number of outer-shell electrons, so they share chemical behaviour. Across a period the number of outer electrons changes at every step, so the chemistry changes too.

misconceptions.question: Lithium, sodium and potassium are all in Group 1. Do they react with water in exactly the same way?
misconceptions.correct: They react in a similar way, producing hydrogen and an alkaline solution, but the reactions become more vigorous down the group.
misconceptions.misconception: Elements in the same group are chemically the same, so their reactions are identical and you could not tell one from another by watching.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Similar properties' is compressed to 'the same properties'. The periodic idea of repeating patterns is learnt without the equally important idea of trends within a group.
misconceptions.correction: Periodic relationships include both similarity and trend. All Group 1 metals give a metal hydroxide and hydrogen with water, but lithium fizzes steadily, sodium melts into a ball, and potassium ignites - a clear trend down the group.

misconceptions.question: What do the atoms of elements in the same group actually have in common?
misconceptions.correct: They have the same number of electrons in their outer shell, not the same total number of electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Elements in the same group have the same number of electrons, which is why they behave in the same way in reactions.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The rule is often shortened in notes to 'same number of electrons', dropping the crucial words 'in the outer shell'. Since group number can be read straight off the table, students do not check what it counts.
misconceptions.correction: A lithium atom has 3 electrons in total and a sodium atom has 11, so their totals differ. Each has one electron in its outer shell, and that shared outer arrangement is what makes their chemistry alike.

misconceptions.question: Why is potassium more reactive than lithium?
misconceptions.correct: A potassium atom is larger, so its single outer electron is further from the nucleus and shielded by more inner shells, and is therefore lost more easily.
misconceptions.misconception: Potassium has more electrons than lithium, so it has more electrons available to give away, which makes it react more strongly.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'More reactive' is read as 'more to give'. The idea that reactivity depends on how easily one electron is lost, not on how many electrons exist, has to be taught explicitly.
misconceptions.correction: Both metals lose exactly one electron and form 1+ ions. What changes down the group is the strength of the attraction on that outer electron: greater distance and more shielding mean weaker attraction, so it is lost more readily.

misconceptions.question: In sodium chloride, what holds the sodium and the chlorine together?
misconceptions.correct: Sodium transfers an electron to chlorine, and the resulting Na+ and Cl- ions are held together by strong electrostatic attraction.
misconceptions.misconception: Sodium gives its electron to chlorine, and then the two atoms are held together by that shared electron sitting between them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Dot-and-cross diagrams put the transferred electron at the boundary between two atoms, which looks like sharing. Students also blur the two bonding routes because both are drawn the same way.
misconceptions.correction: Once the electron has moved, there is nothing shared. Two charged particles are left, and it is the attraction between opposite charges that bonds them. Sharing is a different route, used when two non-metals bond.

misconceptions.question: Is a covalent bond weaker than an ionic bond because the atoms only share?
misconceptions.correct: No. Covalent bonds are strong; the shared pair of electrons is strongly attracted to both nuclei.
misconceptions.misconception: Sharing is a half-hearted sort of bonding, so covalent bonds must be weaker than bonds where an electron is handed over completely.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Simple molecular substances such as chlorine and water have low melting points, and students attribute this to weak covalent bonds instead of to weak forces between whole molecules.
misconceptions.correction: Separate the two things being broken. Melting a simple molecular substance overcomes the weak forces between molecules; the covalent bonds inside each molecule stay intact and are strong.

misconceptions.question: Why do simple molecular substances such as chlorine have low boiling points?
misconceptions.correct: Because the forces between one molecule and the next are weak and need little energy to overcome.
misconceptions.misconception: The covalent bonds in the molecules are weak, so only a small amount of energy is needed to break them and boil the substance.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Weak' is attached to the only bond the student can see drawn. The intermolecular forces are usually invisible on a diagram, so they are not available as an explanation.
misconceptions.correction: State which force is overcome. Boiling separates whole molecules from each other, so the weak forces between molecules are overcome. The strong covalent bonds inside each molecule are not broken at all.

misconceptions.question: Why is graphite soft enough to write with?
misconceptions.correct: Graphite is made of layers of carbon atoms with no covalent bonds between the layers, so the layers can slide over one another.
misconceptions.misconception: The covalent bonds in graphite are weak, which is why the structure gives way so easily when you press a pencil onto paper.
misconceptions.whyItArises: A soft substance is assumed to have weak bonds throughout. The distinction between bonding within a layer and the lack of bonding between layers is easy to miss on a two-dimensional diagram.
misconceptions.correction: Within each layer every carbon atom is joined to three others by strong covalent bonds. It is the absence of covalent bonds between layers that lets them slide, which is arrangement, not bond strength.

misconceptions.question: Diamond and graphite both contain only carbon atoms. Should they behave the same?
misconceptions.correct: No. Their atoms are arranged differently, and arrangement decides behaviour, so their properties are very different.
misconceptions.misconception: Substances made of the same element must have the same properties, because the properties come from what the atoms are.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Students learn that properties depend on the element, which works well for comparing different elements and hides the fact that structure matters just as much.
misconceptions.correction: In diamond each carbon atom forms four covalent bonds in a rigid three-dimensional network, giving a very hard substance that does not conduct. In graphite each carbon forms three bonds in sliding layers with delocalised electrons, so it is soft and conducts.

misconceptions.question: Is sodium chloride made of NaCl molecules?
misconceptions.correct: No. It is a giant lattice of Na+ and Cl- ions; the formula NaCl gives the ratio of ions, not the size of a particle.
misconceptions.misconception: The formula NaCl means one sodium joined to one chlorine, so the substance is made of separate NaCl molecules packed together.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Formulae are first met for molecules such as H2O and CO2, where the formula does count the atoms in one particle. The same reading is then applied to ionic formulae.
misconceptions.correction: Ask what the formula counts. In a giant ionic structure it counts a ratio: one Na+ for every Cl-, repeated through a lattice of millions of ions. That is why the melting point is 801 degrees C rather than the low value a molecular substance would have.

misconceptions.question: How does a catalyst make a reaction go faster?
misconceptions.correct: It provides a different reaction pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions succeed.
misconceptions.misconception: A catalyst gives the reacting particles extra energy, so more of them have enough energy to get over the barrier and react.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Any change that speeds a reaction up is assumed to work by adding energy, because that is how heating works, and heating is the first rate factor students meet.
misconceptions.correction: A catalyst changes the height of the barrier, not the energy of the particles. The same particles, at the same temperature, now meet a lower activation energy, so more of their collisions are successful.

misconceptions.question: Why does heating a reaction mixture increase the rate so much?
misconceptions.correct: Mainly because a greater proportion of colliding particles have energy above the activation energy, and also because collisions become more frequent.
misconceptions.misconception: Heating works because the particles move faster and bump into each other more often - collision frequency is the whole story.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Particles move faster' is a satisfying and visual explanation that answers the question well enough at first sight, so the energy half of the argument is dropped.
misconceptions.correction: Give both parts, and rank them. More frequent collisions help a little; the large effect comes from the fact that many more collisions now carry enough energy to cross the activation energy barrier.

misconceptions.question: If a reaction gives out energy, does it still need energy to get going?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. Every reaction has an activation energy barrier, including exothermic reactions.
misconceptions.misconception: Exothermic reactions release energy, so they must be able to start on their own without any energy being supplied first.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Overall energy change and activation energy are two different quantities on the same reaction profile, and students who have only met the overall change use it to answer both questions.
misconceptions.correction: Methane burning is strongly exothermic, but a gas ring still needs a spark. The spark supplies the activation energy; once the reaction starts, the energy it releases keeps supplying the barrier for further reaction.

misconceptions.question: Does the activation energy tell you how much energy a reaction gives out?
misconceptions.correct: No. Activation energy is the minimum energy needed for colliding particles to react; it is not the energy released.
misconceptions.misconception: Activation energy is the energy the reaction produces once it is activated, so a big activation energy means a lot of energy given out.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Both quantities are energies measured in the same units and drawn on the same diagram, and the word 'activation' sounds like something the reaction produces rather than something it demands.
misconceptions.correction: Read the profile carefully. Activation energy is the height of the hump from the reactants; the energy given out is the drop from reactants to products. A reaction can have a large barrier and a small energy change, or the reverse.

misconceptions.question: In proton transfer, do protons really move out of an atom's nucleus?
misconceptions.correct: No. The particle transferred is a hydrogen ion, H+, which is a whole hydrogen nucleus moving between substances; no other nucleus is changed.
misconceptions.misconception: Transferring a proton means taking a proton out of a nucleus, so the atom would turn into a different element during the reaction.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Protons have been taught as nuclear particles that define the element, so 'proton transfer' sounds nuclear. Students correctly know that changing the proton number changes the element, and then apply it in the wrong place.
misconceptions.correction: A hydrogen atom is one proton with one electron. Take the electron away and the proton is the whole ion, H+, so a hydrogen ion can be handed from one substance to another. Chemical reactions never alter the nucleus of any other atom.

misconceptions.question: What exactly is the H+ ion that acids produce in solution?
misconceptions.correct: A hydrogen atom that has lost its only electron, leaving a single proton.
misconceptions.misconception: H+ is a hydrogen atom carrying a positive charge, and it still has its electron like other ions do.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Other common ions, such as Na+ and Ca2+, keep plenty of electrons after losing one or two, so students generalise that an ion is an atom with electrons still in place.
misconceptions.correction: Hydrogen has only one electron to begin with. Removing it leaves nothing but the nucleus, so H+ is literally a proton. That is why acid reactions are described as proton transfer.

misconceptions.question: Can a reaction be an oxidation if no oxygen is involved?
misconceptions.correct: Yes. In terms of electrons, oxidation is the loss of electrons, whether or not oxygen takes part.
misconceptions.misconception: Oxidation must involve oxygen, because that is what the word means, so a reaction with no oxygen cannot be an oxidation.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The word contains 'oxygen', and the first examples taught are metals burning in air, so the definition in terms of oxygen is learnt first and never widened.
misconceptions.correction: The electron definition is the general one. When sodium reacts with chlorine, each sodium atom loses an electron and is oxidised, even though no oxygen is present anywhere in the reaction.

misconceptions.question: In terms of electrons, which is oxidation and which is reduction?
misconceptions.correct: Oxidation is loss of electrons and reduction is gain of electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Reduction means the number of electrons is reduced, so reduction must be losing electrons and oxidation must be gaining them.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Reduction' invites the reading 'something goes down', and the electron count is the obvious thing to reduce. The charge on the ion does fall, which makes the wrong reasoning feel confirmed.
misconceptions.correction: Use OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain, of electrons. What is reduced is the charge, not the number of electrons: gaining electrons takes Cu2+ down to Cu.

misconceptions.question: When two non-metals react, must one of them lose electrons to the other?
misconceptions.correct: No. Non-metals react with each other by sharing electrons and forming covalent bonds.
misconceptions.misconception: Reactions work by one atom giving electrons and another taking them, so in any reaction one substance must lose electrons completely.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Electron transfer is taught first and with vivid examples such as sodium and chlorine, so it becomes the model for all reactions. Electron sharing is then treated as a description of bonds rather than as a way reactions happen.
misconceptions.correction: Electron sharing is one of the three ways reactions take place in its own right. When hydrogen reacts with chlorine to give hydrogen chloride, the atoms share pairs of electrons; no ions are formed.

misconceptions.question: There are many named types of reaction. How can there be only three ways?
misconceptions.correct: The familiar names describe recognisable patterns, but the underlying change in each is proton transfer, electron transfer or electron sharing.
misconceptions.misconception: Combustion, neutralisation, displacement and thermal decomposition are all different ways of reacting, so there must be far more than three.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The named reaction types are how reactions are taught and classified throughout the course, so they feel like the fundamental categories rather than useful labels for patterns of behaviour.
misconceptions.correction: The names classify what a reaction looks like; the three ways classify what happens to the particles. Neutralisation is proton transfer, displacement of a metal is electron transfer, and non-metals combining is electron sharing.

misconceptions.question: Are proton transfer and electron transfer just two names for the same idea?
misconceptions.correct: No. They move different particles: proton transfer moves H+ ions, electron transfer moves electrons.
misconceptions.misconception: Both are called transfer and both involve charged particles, so they amount to the same kind of change described in two ways.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The shared word 'transfer' and the shared idea of charge blur the two, especially when both are met in quick succession in a summary list.
misconceptions.correction: Check what moves. In an acid-alkali reaction an H+ ion moves and no element changes its charge otherwise; when magnesium burns, electrons move from magnesium to oxygen and both change charge.

misconceptions.question: Does an exothermic reaction create energy?
misconceptions.correct: No. It transfers energy to the surroundings; energy is conserved and can be neither created nor destroyed.
misconceptions.misconception: Exothermic reactions make new energy, which is why the surroundings get hotter than before the reaction started.
misconceptions.whyItArises: From the outside the energy appears from nowhere, and everyday language about a fire 'producing' or 'generating' heat encourages the idea that energy is manufactured.
misconceptions.correction: The energy was already stored in the chemicals. The reaction transfers it to the surroundings, so the store in the chemicals falls by exactly as much as the surroundings gain.

misconceptions.question: Where does the energy go in an endothermic reaction?
misconceptions.correct: It is taken in from the surroundings, which is why the temperature of the surroundings falls; none of it is destroyed.
misconceptions.misconception: The energy is used up and lost during an endothermic reaction, and that loss is what makes the temperature drop.
misconceptions.whyItArises: 'Used up' is how students describe fuels and batteries in everyday life, and a falling temperature looks like evidence that energy has gone out of existence.
misconceptions.correction: Follow the energy rather than the temperature. Energy moves out of the surroundings and into the chemicals, so the surroundings cool while the store in the chemicals rises. The total is unchanged.

misconceptions.question: If energy is conserved, how can the temperature change at all?
misconceptions.correct: Conservation means the total is unchanged, not that nothing moves; a temperature change shows energy has been transferred between chemicals and surroundings.
misconceptions.misconception: If energy cannot be created or destroyed, then the amount of energy everywhere stays the same, so the thermometer should not move.
misconceptions.whyItArises: Conservation is heard as 'nothing changes'. Students do not distinguish between the total energy, which is fixed, and where the energy is, which is exactly what a reaction alters.
misconceptions.correction: Conserved means accounted for, not stationary. A rising thermometer shows energy has moved from the chemicals into the surroundings; a falling one shows it has moved the other way.

misconceptions.question: Is the mass of an atom what decides how the element behaves chemically?
misconceptions.correct: No. Chemical behaviour is decided by electronic structure, above all by the number of electrons in the outer shell.
misconceptions.misconception: The elements are set out in order of how heavy their atoms are, so mass must be the property that explains the patterns and trends in the table.
misconceptions.whyItArises: The relative atomic mass is the largest number printed in most periodic table boxes, and mass does increase steadily in the same direction as several trends, so correlation looks like cause. Mendeleev's early table really was ordered by mass, which reinforces the idea.
misconceptions.correction: The modern periodic table is arranged in order of atomic number, and that number fixes how many electrons an atom has and how they are arranged. Mass rises alongside many trends, but it is the electronic structure that does the explaining.

mcqs.stem: Which statement about atoms and elements is correct?

options.text: Matter is made of tiny particles called atoms, and about 100 types occur naturally.
options.rationale: Matter is composed of tiny particles called atoms, and there are about 100 different naturally occurring types of atom, which are the elements.

options.text: Matter is made of atoms, and about 100 different substances exist in total.
options.rationale: A student who reads 'about 100' as a limit on substances rather than on types of atom accepts this figure without noticing it contradicts the millions of known compounds.

options.text: Matter is made of atoms, and every element shown in the periodic table occurs naturally.
options.rationale: The periodic table is presented as one finished object, so students assume nature supplies every box in it.

options.text: Matter is made of atoms, and one type of atom exists for each known compound.
options.rationale: Students who have not separated element from compound imagine a dedicated particle for every substance, which is how they explain the variety of matter.

mcqs.stem: Millions of different compounds are known, yet there are only about 100 naturally occurring elements. How is this possible?

options.text: New types of atom are created every time a new compound is made.
options.rationale: Students who cannot see how 100 ingredients give millions of products invent new ingredients to close the gap.

options.text: Atoms of those elements combine in a huge variety of ratios and arrangements.
options.rationale: A limited set of building blocks gives an unlimited set of products, because atoms can join in different numbers, ratios and arrangements.

options.text: Most compounds contain elements that are not in the periodic table.
options.rationale: If the table is thought to list only the familiar elements, students assume the rest of chemistry is made from something not shown.

options.text: Compounds are only mixtures, so they are not limited by the elements.
options.rationale: The compound-mixture distinction is fragile, and treating compounds as mixtures appears to remove any restriction on how many can exist.

mcqs.stem: What does it mean to say that the elements show periodic relationships in their properties?

options.text: Every element in the same period of the table has very similar chemical properties.
options.rationale: 'Periodic' contains the word period, so students attach the similarity to rows instead of columns.

options.text: All elements in one group behave identically, so their reactions look the same.
options.rationale: 'Similar properties' is compressed to 'the same properties', and the trend down a group is lost.

options.text: Similar chemical and physical properties recur at regular intervals across the elements.
options.rationale: This is what 'periodic' means: arrange the elements in order of atomic number and similar properties come round again and again.

options.text: The properties of the elements change smoothly right across the whole table.
options.rationale: Students who remember 'trends in the periodic table' but not repetition picture one continuous gradient from hydrogen onwards.

mcqs.stem: Lithium, sodium and potassium all react with water to give hydrogen and an alkaline solution. Which statement best explains this?

options.text: They are in the same period, so their chemical properties are bound to match.
options.rationale: Group and period are routinely swapped, and the claim sounds like the rule the student half-remembers.

options.text: They react at exactly the same rate, because group members are chemically the same.
options.rationale: Students who read similarity as identity see no reason for the reactions to differ in vigour.

options.text: They are metals, and every metal in the periodic table reacts with water like this.
options.rationale: Group 1 is the only set of metals many students have seen reacting with water, so it becomes their model for metals in general.

options.text: They are in the same group, so they share a repeating pattern of chemical properties.
options.rationale: Group members have the same number of outer-shell electrons, which is why their chemical behaviour is alike.

mcqs.stem: Why can the periodic properties of the elements be explained by atomic structure?

options.text: Because chemical properties depend on the number of neutrons in the nucleus.
options.rationale: Neutrons are the particle students least understand, so they are a common default when a nuclear explanation is expected.

options.text: Because chemical properties depend on the number of electrons in the outer shell.
options.rationale: Outer-shell electrons are the electrons involved in bonding, so the repeating pattern of outer-shell arrangements gives the repeating pattern of properties.

options.text: Because chemical properties depend on the total number of electrons an atom contains.
options.rationale: The rule is often shortened to 'same number of electrons', so the total is taken to be what matters.

options.text: Because chemical properties depend on how heavy the atom is compared to others.
options.rationale: Relative atomic mass is the number printed most prominently in each box, so students reach for it as the property that must be doing the work.

mcqs.stem: Potassium reacts with water far more vigorously than lithium does. Which explanation is correct?

options.text: A potassium atom has more electrons in total, so it has more of them to give away.
options.rationale: 'More reactive' is read as 'more to give', which fits the larger electron count neatly.

options.text: A potassium atom has more outer-shell electrons than lithium, so it reacts faster.
options.rationale: Students who do not track which electrons the group number counts assume a bigger atom must have a fuller outer shell.

options.text: Potassium has a larger relative atomic mass, and heavier atoms always react faster.
options.rationale: The mass number increases down the group alongside reactivity, so correlation is mistaken for cause.

options.text: Potassium's outer electron is further from the nucleus and shielded, so it is lost easily.
options.rationale: Both metals lose one electron; greater distance and more shielding weaken the attraction on it, so it is lost more readily.

mcqs.stem: According to this key idea, what are the two ways in which atoms bond together?

options.text: Electrons are shared between atoms, or protons are transferred between atoms.
options.rationale: Proton transfer appears elsewhere in the same list of key ideas, so students import it into the account of bonding.

options.text: Atoms are held by attraction between their nuclei, or by their opposite charges.
options.rationale: Bonding is known to involve attraction, and the nucleus is the most obvious charged part of an atom to attribute it to.

options.text: Electrons are transferred from one atom to another, or electrons are shared.
options.rationale: The specification states that atoms bond either by transferring electrons from one atom to another or by sharing electrons.

options.text: Electrons are transferred to fill outer shells, or the atoms simply stick together.
options.rationale: Students who see only transfer as real bonding treat covalent bonding as a vaguer kind of sticking.

mcqs.stem: Magnesium reacts with oxygen to form magnesium oxide, MgO. Which description of the bonding is correct?

options.text: Each magnesium atom shares two electrons with an oxygen atom, making two bonds.
options.rationale: Sharing is the route drawn most often in lessons, and a two-electron change looks like a double bond to a student who has not checked that magnesium is a metal.

options.text: Each magnesium atom transfers two electrons to oxygen, giving Mg2+ and O2- ions.
options.rationale: A metal reacting with a non-metal bonds by electron transfer; magnesium loses two electrons to form Mg2+ and oxygen gains them to form O2-.

options.text: Each magnesium atom gains two electrons from an oxygen atom, giving Mg2- ions.
options.rationale: Students who reverse loss and gain put the electrons on the wrong atom and produce a negative metal ion without noticing.

options.text: Each magnesium atom transfers two protons to an oxygen atom, giving charged ions.
options.rationale: Once 'transfer' is separated from 'electron', the proton is the charged particle students name, since charge is what they know ions have.

mcqs.stem: Chlorine boils at -34 degrees C, but silicon dioxide melts above 1600 degrees C. Which statement explains the difference?

options.text: The covalent bonds inside chlorine molecules are far weaker than those in silicon dioxide.
options.rationale: The covalent bond is the only force on the diagram, so a low boiling point is blamed on it.

options.text: Silicon dioxide contains ionic bonds, and ionic bonding is always stronger than covalent.
options.rationale: High melting point is associated with ionic compounds, so students infer the bonding backwards from the data.

options.text: Chlorine is a gas, and gases always have weaker bonds than solids at room temperature.
options.rationale: State of matter is treated as a property of the bonding itself rather than a consequence of the forces between particles.

options.text: Chlorine exists as small molecules with weak forces between them; silicon dioxide is giant.
options.rationale: Boiling chlorine only overcomes weak forces between molecules, while melting silicon dioxide breaks strong covalent bonds throughout a giant structure.

mcqs.stem: Diamond and graphite both contain only carbon atoms, yet graphite is soft and conducts electricity. Why?

options.text: The covalent bonds in graphite are weak, so its atoms slide and its electrons move.
options.rationale: Softness is assumed to require weak bonds, and the bonds within the layers are the only ones a student can see.

options.text: Graphite must contain a different element from diamond, which changes its properties.
options.rationale: If properties are believed to come only from the element, different properties force the student to invent a different element.

options.text: The carbon atoms are arranged in layers with delocalised electrons between them.
options.rationale: Layers with no covalent bonds between them can slide, and the delocalised electrons are free to move and carry charge; the arrangement decides the behaviour.

options.text: Graphite is a metallic form of carbon, so free electrons let it conduct and bend.
options.rationale: Conducting is strongly associated with metals, so a conducting non-metal is reclassified rather than explained.

mcqs.stem: Ice melts at 0 degrees C but sodium chloride melts at 801 degrees C. Which statement explains this difference?

options.text: Sodium chloride is a giant lattice of strongly attracted ions; ice is separate molecules.
options.rationale: Melting the lattice must overcome strong electrostatic attraction between millions of ions, while melting ice only overcomes forces between molecules.

options.text: The covalent bonds in water are weaker than the covalent bonds in sodium chloride.
options.rationale: Melting is assumed to break bonds within particles, so the comparison is made between the wrong pair of forces.

options.text: Sodium chloride molecules are far larger and heavier than water molecules are.
options.rationale: Treating NaCl as a molecule makes size the only available explanation for the high melting point.

options.text: Water is a liquid at room temperature, so its particles must be much further apart.
options.rationale: State is used as the explanation rather than the thing to be explained, and particle spacing is confused with force strength.

mcqs.stem: What is meant by the activation energy of a reaction?

options.text: The energy given out to the surroundings when particles collide successfully.
options.rationale: Both quantities are energies on the same diagram, and 'activation' sounds like something the reaction produces.

options.text: The energy that must be supplied by heating before an exothermic reaction starts.
options.rationale: Students who link starting energy only to heating restrict the idea to reactions they have had to warm up.

options.text: The minimum energy that colliding particles must have for a reaction to occur.
options.rationale: Activation energy is the barrier to reaction: collisions carrying less than this energy produce no chemical change.

options.text: The total energy stored in the bonds of the reactants before the reaction begins.
options.rationale: 'Energy of the reactants' is a phrase from reaction profiles, and students attach the label to the nearest quantity they can name.

mcqs.stem: Why does adding a catalyst increase the rate of a reaction?

options.text: It gives the reacting particles extra energy, so more of them are able to react.
options.rationale: Heating is the first rate factor taught, so every other factor is assumed to work by adding energy too.

options.text: It provides a different reaction pathway that has a lower activation energy.
options.rationale: The barrier is lowered rather than the particles changed, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful.

options.text: It increases the number of collisions by making the particles move much faster.
options.rationale: Collision frequency is the explanation students find most vivid, so it is applied to every rate factor.

options.text: It is gradually used up in the reaction, which keeps the mixture warm throughout.
options.rationale: Catalysts are known to be involved in the reaction, and students who have not met 'not used up' assume they behave like a reactant.

mcqs.stem: Why does raising the temperature have such a large effect on the rate of a reaction?

options.text: Heating lowers the activation energy, so the barrier becomes easier to cross.
options.rationale: Students who know the barrier controls rate assume anything that speeds a reaction up must lower it.

options.text: A far greater proportion of collisions now have energy above the barrier.
options.rationale: Higher temperature means more energetic particles, so many more collisions reach the activation energy; this outweighs the increase in collision frequency.

options.text: Heating raises the concentration of the reactants, so more particles are present.
options.rationale: Two separate rate factors are merged, and warming a mixture is imagined to concentrate it.

options.text: The particles collide more often, and that is the only reason the rate rises.
options.rationale: The collision-frequency argument is true as far as it goes, which makes the word 'only' easy to overlook.

mcqs.stem: The specification states that chemical reactions take place in only three different ways. What are they?

options.text: Proton transfer, electron transfer and electron sharing
options.rationale: These are the three ways the specification names immediately after the statement.

options.text: Combustion, neutralisation and thermal decomposition
options.rationale: These are the reaction names used throughout the course, so they feel like the fundamental categories.

options.text: Proton transfer, neutron transfer and electron transfer
options.rationale: A student who remembers only the word 'transfer' completes the list with the three subatomic particles.

options.text: Oxidation, reduction and the neutralisation of an acid
options.rationale: These are the three processes most often named in summary lessons, and two of them do involve electron transfer.

mcqs.stem: Chemists give reactions many names, such as combustion, displacement and neutralisation. How does this fit with there being only three ways?

options.text: The names show that there are many more than three ways for reactions to happen.
options.rationale: The number of familiar labels is taken as direct evidence against the claim in the key idea.

options.text: Each named reaction involves all three of the changes happening one after another.
options.rationale: Students who cannot tell the three changes apart reconcile the two ideas by assuming every reaction uses all of them.

options.text: Only reactions given one of those three names count as reactions at GCSE level.
options.rationale: The key idea is read as a restriction on which reactions are examinable rather than as a claim about mechanism.

options.text: The names describe patterns, but the underlying change is always one of the three.
options.rationale: The names classify what a reaction looks like; the three ways classify what happens to the particles involved.

mcqs.stem: Hydrochloric acid reacts with sodium hydroxide solution. What is transferred in this reaction?

options.text: A whole hydrogen atom, complete with its electron, passes to the hydroxide ion.
options.rationale: Other ions keep most of their electrons, so students assume a hydrogen ion does too.

options.text: A proton leaves the nucleus of a chlorine atom and joins the sodium nucleus.
options.rationale: 'Proton transfer' sounds nuclear, and students correctly know protons live in nuclei.

options.text: A hydrogen ion, H+, which is a single proton, passes to the hydroxide ion.
options.rationale: The acid supplies H+ ions, and each is a hydrogen atom stripped of its one electron, so it is a bare proton; H+ and OH- combine to form water.

options.text: An electron passes from the hydroxide ion to the acid, forming water and salt.
options.rationale: With proton and electron transfer blurred together, the more familiar electron is chosen.

mcqs.stem: Which of these reactions is best described as proton transfer?

options.text: hydrochloric acid + sodium hydroxide, giving sodium chloride and water
options.rationale: An acid reacting with an alkali passes H+ ions to OH- ions, which is proton transfer.

options.text: magnesium + oxygen, when a strip of magnesium burns brightly in air
options.rationale: A student who treats all 'transfer' as one idea picks the reaction where an atom most visibly gives something up.

options.text: zinc + copper sulfate solution, giving zinc sulfate and copper metal
options.rationale: Displacement is a named reaction type, and students who have not linked names to mechanisms guess among them.

options.text: hydrogen + chlorine, when the two gases combine to form hydrogen chloride
options.rationale: Hydrogen is present, so a student looking for 'protons' picks the reaction with hydrogen in it.

mcqs.stem: In terms of electrons, what happens during oxidation and reduction?

options.text: Oxidation is the gain of electrons and reduction is the loss of electrons.
options.rationale: 'Reduction' suggests the number of electrons going down, which reverses the pair.

options.text: Oxidation is the loss of electrons and reduction is the gain of electrons.
options.rationale: This is the electron definition, summarised as OIL RIG: Oxidation Is Loss, Reduction Is Gain.

options.text: Oxidation is the loss of protons and reduction is the gain of protons.
options.rationale: Proton transfer and electron transfer are blurred, so the particle names are interchanged.

options.text: Oxidation is the gain of oxygen only, and electrons are not involved at all.
options.rationale: The word contains 'oxygen' and the earliest examples all involve burning in air.

mcqs.stem: Sodium reacts with chlorine: 2Na + Cl2 gives 2NaCl. Which statement about the electrons is correct?

options.text: Each sodium atom loses one electron and each chlorine atom gains one electron.
options.rationale: Sodium is oxidised to Na+ and chlorine is reduced to Cl-, so the reaction proceeds by electron transfer.

options.text: Each sodium atom gains one electron and each chlorine atom loses one electron.
options.rationale: Loss and gain are reversed, and the student does not check that this would make a metal negative.

options.text: Each sodium atom shares one electron with a chlorine atom, forming a bond.
options.rationale: Sharing is the more familiar picture from dot-and-cross work on molecules, and a metal-non-metal pair is not checked.

options.text: Each sodium atom loses two electrons, which both chlorine atoms then share.
options.rationale: The 2 in front of Na is misread as the number of electrons each sodium atom loses.

mcqs.stem: Nitrogen and hydrogen react to form ammonia: N2 + 3H2 gives 2NH3. How does this reaction take place?

options.text: By electron transfer: nitrogen takes electrons from hydrogen, giving ions.
options.rationale: Electron transfer is taught first and with vivid examples, so it becomes the model for every reaction.

options.text: By proton transfer: hydrogen atoms give their protons to nitrogen atoms.
options.rationale: The presence of hydrogen prompts students to reach for proton transfer, and protons are pictured as detachable.

options.text: By electron sharing: nitrogen and hydrogen atoms share pairs of electrons.
options.rationale: Both elements are non-metals, so they bond by sharing electrons to form covalent bonds in the ammonia molecule.

options.text: By neither: the molecules stick together with no bonds broken or made.
options.rationale: The reaction is reversible and produces a gas from gases, which students read as a physical rather than chemical change.

mcqs.stem: What does the conservation of energy mean for a chemical reaction?

options.text: Energy is transferred between the chemicals and the surroundings, never made.
options.rationale: Energy is conserved in chemical reactions and can be neither created nor destroyed; a reaction only moves it.

options.text: Energy is created by exothermic reactions and destroyed by endothermic ones.
options.rationale: The energy appears from nowhere and vanishes again as far as the observer can tell, and everyday language supports this.

options.text: The temperature of the surroundings cannot change, since energy is conserved.
options.rationale: Conservation is heard as 'nothing changes anywhere' rather than as 'the total is unchanged'.

options.text: Energy is used up as the reaction proceeds, so less exists at the end.
options.rationale: 'Used up' is how fuels and batteries are described in everyday life, and it is transferred to reactions.

mcqs.stem: Citric acid solution is added to sodium hydrogencarbonate and the temperature of the mixture falls. What has happened to the energy?

options.text: Energy has been destroyed by the reaction, which is why the temperature drops.
options.rationale: A falling temperature looks like direct evidence that energy has gone out of existence.

options.text: Energy has been created inside the solution but cannot be felt as warmth.
options.rationale: Students who believe reactions make energy have to explain why none can be detected here.

options.text: The energy of the surroundings is unchanged and the thermometer is misreading.
options.rationale: If conservation is taken to forbid any change, the measurement itself must be wrong.

options.text: Energy has been taken in from the surroundings, so the surroundings cool.
options.rationale: This is an endothermic reaction: energy moves from the surroundings into the chemicals, so the temperature of the surroundings falls.
